implementation_notes: The query object is an expression template rather than a mutable builder: sqlpp11's generated table structs carry the class/field-to-table/column mapping, and select(t.name).from(t).where(t.id == 42) composes a typed expression tree that the connector compiles into SQL with bound parameters, so a query naming a missing column fails to compile. What replaces the classic Query class is value-typed expressions plus operator overloading; a runtime builder stays justified when the query shape is only known at runtime, which is what the sqlite_orm variant covers.
pitfalls: Expression-template errors are notoriously long; wrap recurring shapes in named query functions so call sites stay readable.
The table structs mirror one schema version: a migration that renames a column stops the build until they are updated.
Rendering allocates per call; let the connector's prepared-statement cache key on the expression type instead of rebuilding SQL strings.

variants.name: sqlite_orm runtime statement construction
variants.implementation_notes: sqlite_orm builds statements at runtime from mapped structs and expression objects: storage.get_all<User>(where(c(&User::age) < 30 and c(&User::name) != "Eve")) returns rows, and the where/order_by/limit objects are ordinary values that can be stored, combined and parameterised from user input. It fits when SQLite is the store and the criteria are data-driven, where the compile-time EDSL would need a distinct type for every branch.
variants.code_sketch:
auto rows = storage.get_all<User>(
    where(c(&User::age) >= 18 and c(&User::status) == "active"),
    order_by(&User::name).asc(),
    limit(50));
pitfalls: where(...) expressions hold column pointers: a struct reordered by a refactor silently changes the query.
The DSL is SQLite-specific; porting means rewriting every expression, unlike a dialect-abstracted builder.
